Although the Kharijites received support from oppressed groups in both the countryside and the cities, many members of those same groups were often repelled by the Kharijites’ methods of violence and bloody terror.
There was another positive feature of the Kharijite position: their relative tolerance toward ordinary non-Muslims and non-Arabs.

They were less burdened by religious and ethnic prejudice than many others around them. Relations among them could therefore be based on equality, without distinctions based on blood, ancestry, ethnicity, or religion.
This is striking because it existed alongside their well-known religious rigidity.
Their freedom from these forms of prejudice may have had two causes.

First, after the killing of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, the Kharijites became united above all by one thing: opposition to Umayyad power. This became the main point around which their movement gathered supporters, regardless of identities that might otherwise have divided them.
Second, the Kharijite movement had from the beginning included members of several different tribes. Its organization therefore did not encourage the old tribal rivalries surrounding leadership.
Even so, almost all of the support the Kharijites gained among oppressed Muslims and non-Muslims was concentrated in Iraq and parts of Iran.
In Syria, Umayyad control, together with the power of feudal landlords, large merchants, wealthy local families, and the Kalbite tribes, made it difficult for the Kharijites to build a social base.
The Umayyads used the people of Syria to fight the Kharijites in Iraq and Iran, just as they also used them to fight the Shiʿa there.
When ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān became ruler of the Umayyad state, it faced two major dangers: the Kharijites in Iraq and ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca.
ʿAbd al-Malik decided to destroy Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement first, so that he could then concentrate on the Kharijites.

Once he had defeated Ibn al-Zubayr and destroyed the foundations of his movement, he turned to the other danger and confronted it through repression and terror—the same weapon used by the Kharijites themselves.
But Umayyad repression soon went far beyond the Kharijites. It spread across Iraqi society, especially among peasants and the poorest and weakest sections of the population.
Before this, Iraq had been governed on behalf of the Umayyads by a man who leaned toward Ibn al-Zubayr and was sympathetic to both Kharijite and Shiʿi opposition to Umayyad rule.
This led ʿAbd al-Malik to choose a new governor for Iraq who would be exceptionally ruthless and firmly loyal to the Umayyads.

He needed someone who would not be influenced by Iraq’s political environment, which at the time was divided among supporters of the Shiʿa, the Kharijites, and Ibn al-Zubayr—especially in Kufa, then the capital of Iraq.
Al-Ḥajjāj was the man ʿAbd al-Malik chose for this dangerous task.
First, al-Ḥajjāj was strongly loyal to the Umayyads.
Second, he had a forceful personality and was prepared to use violence against his opponents.
Third, he was a powerful speaker who knew how to play on the emotions of his listeners through the language of force and fear.
Al-Ḥajjāj began his rule in Kufa, then Iraq’s leading city.

Kufa was a center of the various forms of “counterrevolution” against the Umayyads. It was also a major center of intellectual life and a breeding ground for ideological conflict between political movements.
At first, al-Ḥajjāj succeeded in terrifying the people of Kufa.
He gathered their leaders in the historic mosque of the city and addressed them in a language of force and threat.
His first speech became famous in the political and literary history of Iraq. Its effect was so strong that no one present dared answer him. They responded only with complete silence.
But the effect did not last.
Political opposition, both Shiʿi and Kharijite, soon became active again. Even al-Ḥajjāj’s terror could not destroy it while he remained in Kufa.

Kharijite uprisings made his position there so insecure that he eventually moved his base to another location on the Tigris in southern Iraq, where he could establish a stronger strategic center for fighting the opposition.
There he founded the city that became permanently associated with his reign of terror: Wāsiṭ.
For twenty years, al-Ḥajjāj ruled the Iraqis through repression and fear.
When he died, Arab historians estimated that the prisons of Iraq held fifty thousand male opponents and thirty thousand women.
His strategy was to subject the entire population of Iraq to violent terror without distinction.
His rule resembled what we today might call martial law or a permanent state of emergency.
Every citizen was treated as guilty until proven innocent. In practice, no one was ever proven innocent.
It was even said that there were not enough executioners to kill the number of people condemned to death.
If we accept the figures given by Arab historians, around 130,000 people were executed in Iraq during his rule.
Peasants, agricultural workers, the urban poor, and craftsmen suffered most under al-Ḥajjāj.
They were crushed by arbitrary taxation, forced labor, imprisonment, and hunger.
Peasants abandoned the land and fled to the cities, only to find repression following them there.

Those who remained on the land were forced to work on irrigation systems. They were also prevented from selling their livestock even when they needed to sell them in order to pay their taxes or meet their most basic needs.
It is true that al-Ḥajjāj did a great deal to expand cultivated land and improve irrigation in Iraq.
But his oppression of the peasants undermined the purpose of those reforms.

The land was not developed enough even to provide the state with the agricultural taxes it needed. In this way, his policies slowed the development of the productive forces and even threatened them with collapse.
This helps explain the peasant uprisings against al-Ḥajjāj.
It also explains why the Kharijite call to fight the Umayyads found such a wide response among the peasants.
The Kharijites were even able to lead some of these uprisings themselves.
But violent repression crushed every uprising that took place during al-Ḥajjāj’s rule.
It also weakened the Kharijites so badly that they were never again able to rebuild their strength or spread their movement on the same scale.
After al-Ḥajjāj, only weakened remnants of the movement remained. These later split into several separate groups, weakening them still further.
5 - The Intellectual War Against the Kharijites
Al-Ḥajjāj’s repression was not the only reason the Kharijites declined and their theory of faith failed to spread.
They were fought intellectually just as seriously as they were fought by the swords of al-Ḥajjāj and the Umayyads.
They faced both kinds of attack at the same time: polemical argument and theoretical criticism.
At first, their fiercest opponents were the Shiʿa.

One important Shiʿi opponent was al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, a son of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya and therefore a grandson of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—the same ʿAlī whom the Kharijites had fought under their slogan:
“Judgment belongs to God, not to ʿAlī.”
Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya confronted the Kharijite theory of faith with an opposing principle.
The Kharijites argued that committing a sin destroyed a person’s faith and made the sinner an unbeliever, because for them faith did not exist without action that matched belief.
Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya answered that sin does not cancel faith.
Like the other Shiʿa, he did not consider action to be one of the elements that make up faith itself.
Someone who commits a sin, even a major one, has violated religious law. But that person remains a believer as long as he continues to believe in the basic principles of Islam.
Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya was not alone in holding this view.
What matters here is the active role he played in opposing the Kharijite theory.

He sent letters to people across the lands under Arab-Islamic rule, openly condemning the Kharijite position, calling on people to reject it, and defending the wider Muslim distinction between inward faith and outward action.

By the end of the first Islamic century and the beginning of the second—that is, between the seventh and eighth centuries CE—many jurists and theologians had joined the intellectual struggle against the Kharijites.
Historians of the period mention among the most important of them Abū Ḥanīfa al-Nuʿmān, the founder of the Sunni school later named after him, the Ḥanafī school, who died in 150 AH / 767 CE.
All of these thinkers agreed that a person who committed a major sin should not be declared an unbeliever or condemned to eternal punishment in hell.
6 - The Political Roots of the Theory of Faith

The debate over whether someone who committed a major sin should be declared an unbeliever became one of the central concerns of Arab-Islamic intellectual life between the seventh and eighth centuries CE.
This debate produced concepts and theories that continued to develop and become intertwined with other intellectual questions until they eventually helped prepare the ground for Arab philosophy.
The issue itself later became one of the central questions of kalām once theology had developed into a distinct field.
We have already seen that the Kharijite movement itself emerged from its position on this very question.
They fought ʿAlī and the Umayyads because this theory led them to declare both groups, and others as well, unbelievers and therefore legitimate targets of armed struggle.
The Shiʿa took a different position.
Other groups among the Prophet’s Companions also held different views on the status of someone who committed a major sin.
The debate over this question was therefore closely tied to the first divisions between Islamic schools and to the emergence of the earliest sectarian movements.
What can we learn from the fact that Arab-Islamic thought became so deeply occupied with this question that it became the first major center of intellectual debate at the time?
A first look at everything we have discussed so far is enough to show that real historical conditions were driving every position and every line of thought in this debate.
We will later see that even the Muʿtazilite movement originally grew out of the dispute over the person who commits a major sin.
Most historians trace the later beginning of the Muʿtazila to the moment when Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ withdrew from the teaching circle of his teacher al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.
But even this later beginning, as we will see, had at its center the disagreement between teacher and student over the person who commits a major sin.

To understand why this question became one of the first major forces driving intellectual life at the end of the seventh century, we therefore need to return to the first historical event in which political conflict between the emerging parties became openly violent and bloody.
That event was the killing of ʿUthmān, the third Rightly Guided Caliph, followed by the transfer of the caliphate, through the principle of consultation, to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
The debate over the person who commits a major sin began from this event.
At first, however, it was not expressed as a theoretical debate about the meaning of faith.
That happened only with the rise of the Kharijites. They were the first to turn the issue into an explicit theory of faith.
When Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr went to war against ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in the Battle of the Camel, their argument was that ʿAlī was one of those responsible for the killing of ʿUthmān.
He therefore had to be fought, because he was a killer, and killing was one of the major sins.
In other words, these two Companions were already thinking along lines that the Kharijites would later express in a more developed theoretical form.

It is true that Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr’s decision to fight ʿAlī was fundamentally a political one. It was also shaped by their personal position toward ʿAlī himself, since he stood as the strongest obstacle to their own political ambitions.
But we also have to remember who Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr were.
They had been close Companions of the Prophet and had reached leading positions within the Islamic movement.
Men of their standing could not easily go to war against someone with the standing of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib unless they could support their position with some principle drawn from Islam itself.
Otherwise, their action would have had no convincing religious justification.

Their claim that ʿAlī was one of those responsible for killing ʿUthmān, and that a killer had committed a major sin, therefore became the justification for launching the Battle of the Camel against him.
